problem: Deep RL navigation policies such as DQN mix policy dynamics and reward attribution inside one black-box Q-network. When fine-tuned on a new maze or goal they forget the old task, and alternatives like Progressive Networks need a representation set that keeps growing. Classical navigation, in turn, needs explicit SLAM, localization and planning, often with human setup.
motivation: A robot should adapt quickly to changed goals or environments while keeping earlier solutions, with limited memory and no explicit localization, mapping or planning. Successor representation learning factors Q into expected discounted future features (dynamics) times reward weights (task). Prior deep successor RL used this only for reward changes; the authors observe that it can be extended to changes in the environment and dynamics as well.
key_idea: Extend deep successor-feature RL to sequential transfer across different maze environments. Each new task's CNN features and successor features are fine-tuned from the previous task, while learned linear maps B^i send current features back to every old task's feature space, so old tasks' Q-functions stay computable.
insight: Decoupling Q into successor features ψ (policy dynamics) and a reward vector ω (Q ≈ ψᵀω) makes transfer structured: adapt only ω when rewards change, ψ when dynamics change, or both. Regressing old-task features through the linear maps B^i works like distillation and forces one shared CNN to keep representing all tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting. Table I supports this: after Map1→Map2 transfer, SF-RL-Transfer still solves Map1 at 50/50 (reward 0.733), while DQN-Finetune drops to 48/50 (reward 0.398, 15.0 steps). After Map3→Map4, DQN-Finetune solves only 4/50 of Map3 while SF-RL keeps 50/50. A post-hoc probe (a 2-hidden-layer network regressing ground-truth pose from φ) shows the learned features implicitly encode robot pose.
method: Feature encoder φ (θφ): a 3-conv-layer CNN (32 8×8/s4, 64 4×4/s2, 64 3×3/s1) plus FC-512, fed a stack of the 4 most recent 64×64 frames.
Reward regression + auto-encoder: R(s) ≈ φ_sᵀω, and a 5-layer deconvolutional decoder d(φ_s) reconstructs s so the features stay representative of the state (Eq. 6).

Successor feature network ψ (θψ, 2 FC layers): outputs ψ(φ_s, a) for each action and is trained by DQN-style Q-learning with φ as the 'reward', γψ(φ_s', a*) as target, and a target network replaced every 5000 steps (Eq. 5). Actions are chosen greedily by Q = ψᵀω.

Sequential transfer: for task k, θφ^k and θψ^k are initialized from task k-1 and trained with Eqs. 9-10. Linear maps B^i (i<k) are learned so that φ^i_s ≈ B^i φ^k_s, and old-task Q^i is recovered as (B^i ψ^{π_i}(φ^k_s,a))ᵀω^i (Eqs. 7-8).

Multi-head old-task successor features: one network with multiple output layers estimates the expectations of current features under old-task policies, using current-task samples only. Overhead is k-1 matrices plus one ω per task.

Sim-to-real depth transfer: the model is pre-trained on rendered Kinect depth in simulated Map5, then transferred to real depth images pre-recorded at all reachable poses of real Map6 (100 noisy images per position and direction).

setting.backbone: Custom CNN encoder (3 conv + FC-512) + deconv decoder + 2-layer FC successor-feature net + linear reward weights, trained from scratch with deep RL (successor-feature Q-learning)
setting.training_data: Online RL interaction in custom simulated 3D mazes (Map1-Map5); learning starts after 3e4 steps with one minibatch of 64 every 4 steps. Real-world transfer uses pre-recorded Kinect depth images at all reachable positions and directions of the real Map6 (100 randomly perturbed images per position and direction); satisfactory after ~60,000 iterations, about 8 h of real experience at 2 Hz.
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (64×64, stack of 4 frames) in simulation; Kinect depth images for the depth and real-robot experiments
setting.action_space: 4 discrete actions: stand still, turn left 90°, turn right 90°, go straight 1 m (continuous motion with Gaussian control noise in sim)
setting.simulator: custom 3D maze robot simulator (simulated Pioneer-3dx, differential drive); real Robotino maze
setting.privileged: none at test time (no localization or map); the goal is fixed per task through the reward, and training rewards use simulator ground truth (goal/collision)

numbers_note: All results are on the authors' own simulated mazes and a real maze, not a standard benchmark. The only table (Table I) reports re-evaluation on the base maps (Map1, Map3) after transfer. Learning curves for the transfer targets Map2 and Map4 (Fig. 6), the depth sim-to-real transfer to Map6 (Fig. 8) and pose-regression results (Fig. 4) appear only in figures. Real-robot tests on Map6 and Map7 are shown only in a video. Success counts are printed as 'N/50' ratios and are kept in 'extra' rather than converted to percentages.
results: SF-RL-Transfer reaches near-optimal performance on new mazes much faster than SF-RL from scratch; on Map2 it learns about as fast as a supervised A* imitator. It is comparable to DQN-Finetune in transfer speed and faster than DQN-FixFeature, though DQN from scratch is slightly faster than SF-RL from scratch. Unlike DQN-Finetune it keeps old tasks. On Map1 after Map2 transfer it gets 50/50 successes with reward 0.733 (A* 0.814), versus DQN-Finetune's 48/50 with reward 0.398. On Map3 after Map4 transfer it gets 50/50 versus DQN-Finetune's 4/50. Transfer from simulated depth to real Kinect depth gives a large speed-up, reaching satisfactory performance at ~60k iterations (~8 h of real experience).
limitations: Only small, simple maze-like environments with a single fixed goal per task (the goal is encoded in the reward, not goal-conditioned); the evaluation is small-scale (50 starts) on custom maps with no standard benchmark.

Old-task successor features are estimated from current-task samples under an assumed linear feature relation B^i, relying on strong overlap between tasks. The authors note that tasks with no shared structure would need more parameters, and partial observability is handled only by 4-frame stacking.
Real-world training used pre-recorded depth images at discretized reachable poses rather than online real interaction; the real-robot evaluation is reported only qualitatively (video).
